figureFiles.caption: A heat engine between steam at 823 K and a condenser at 319 K, drawn per 100 MJ of heat supplied. The first law says work plus rejected heat equals heat supplied; the second law says the rejected heat must carry away the entropy, which caps the work at 1 − 319/823 = 61 percent of the heat.

Left: the four components of a Rankine plant with state points 1 to 4. Right: the same ideal cycle on a temperature-entropy diagram, plotted from steam-property data for 10 MPa, 550 °C and a 10 kPa condenser. Most of the heat enters while the water warms and boils at 311 °C, so the mean temperature of heat addition (dashed line) is only 267 °C.

Gas-turbine exhaust at roughly 600 °C raises steam in a heat-recovery steam generator. Gas flows toward the stack while feedwater enters at the cool end, so the two streams run in counterflow. The energy figures are rounded values for a modern H-class plant with one gas turbine and one steam turbine.

lesson.hook: In 1824 a 28-year-old French military engineer, Sadi Carnot, paid to print 600 copies of a 118-page booklet, *Réflexions sur la puissance motrice du feu*. Hardly anyone read it, and Carnot died of cholera in 1832, aged 36. His booklet nonetheless contained an idea that every power plant still obeys: the work you can get from heat is limited by the temperatures between which the heat flows. Almost two centuries later, in March 2018, Guinness World Records recognized Chubu Electric’s Nishi-Nagoya Block 1 in Japan, built around GE 7HA gas turbines, as the world’s most efficient combined-cycle power plant, at 63.08 percent gross efficiency. That plant still sends more than a third of its fuel energy into the air and cooling water. This chapter explains why it must, and why it loses so little compared with the plants that came before it.
lesson.overview: Chapter 1 showed that a large share of primary energy never becomes a useful service, and that most of the “rejected energy” in a Sankey diagram leaves from thermal power plants. This chapter explains that loss from first principles. Section 2.1 sets out the first and second laws, entropy and exergy, the tools for deciding which losses are inevitable and which are engineering choices. Section 2.2 derives the Carnot limit and compares it with real fleet efficiencies. Section 2.3 analyzes the two workhorse cycles, Rankine (steam) and Brayton (gas turbine), with real operating numbers. Section 2.4 combines them into the combined-cycle gas plant, one of our running examples, and asks when cogeneration makes sense. Chapter 4 uses these results for coal, gas and nuclear plants; Chapters 5 and 6 meet converters, such as wind turbines and fuel cells, that are not heat engines and face different limits.
objectives: Apply energy and entropy balances to turbines, boilers and heat engines, and compute exergy and exergy destruction with units at every step.
Calculate the Carnot limit from reservoir temperatures in kelvin and compare it with the measured efficiencies of real plants.
Analyze ideal Rankine and Brayton cycles from property data, including pump and compressor work, and explain their efficiencies through the mean temperature of heat addition.
Derive the combined-cycle relation η_cc = η_B + η_R(1 − η_B), state its assumptions, and use it to explain the efficiency of modern gas plants.
Evaluate a cogeneration scheme with the utilization factor, exergy efficiency and fuel saved against separate production.

sections.title: The first and second laws
reading: Chapter 1 drew energy flows as Sankey diagrams in which every joule entering an economy reappears as a service or as rejected energy. That accounting rests on the **first law of thermodynamics**: energy is neither created nor destroyed, only converted. For a closed system the first law reads ΔE = Q − W, with Q the heat added to the system and W the work it does, both in joules [1]. Power-plant components are better treated as open systems in steady flow. Per kilogram of working fluid, the steady-flow energy equation is q − w = Δh + ΔV²/2 + gΔz, where h is the specific **enthalpy** in kJ/kg [1, 2]. In turbines, pumps and boilers the kinetic and potential energy terms are usually tiny next to Δh, so an adiabatic turbine’s work is simply h_in − h_out. Steam entering at 3,400 kJ/kg and leaving at 2,300 kJ/kg delivers 1,100 kJ/kg; at a flow of 100 kg/s that is 110,000 kJ/s, or 110 MW.

The first law cannot explain the most striking feature of Chapter 1’s Sankey diagrams: fossil and nuclear power plants reject more than half of the energy they take in as low-temperature heat. Energy conservation would be just as happy with a plant that turned all of its fuel into electricity. What forbids that plant is the **second law of thermodynamics**. Rudolf Clausius, in papers from 1850 onward, built the second law on the observation that heat does not pass by itself from a colder body to a hotter one [4]. The equivalent Kelvin–Planck statement is the one a power engineer meets every day: no device operating in a cycle can take heat from a single reservoir and turn all of it into work [1]. Some heat must always be rejected to a colder body. Section 2.2 shows exactly how much.

Clausius gave the quantity behind the second law its name, **entropy**, in 1865 [3]. Entropy S is a property, measured in J/K and defined through reversible heat transfer as dS = δQ_rev/T, with T in kelvin. For any real process the entropy balance is ΔS = ∫δQ/T + S_gen. The **entropy generation** S_gen is zero for an ideal reversible process and positive for every real one; friction, mixing, combustion and heat transfer across a finite temperature difference all generate entropy [1]. Now apply this to a heat engine. Over one cycle the working fluid returns to its starting state, so its entropy change is zero. The entropy brought in with the heat Q_H at temperature T_H, plus everything generated inside, must leave with the rejected heat: Q_C/T_C = Q_H/T_H + S_gen. Rejected heat is not a design flaw. It is the only exit for entropy.

Engineers turn the second law into an accounting tool through **exergy**: the maximum useful work obtainable from a system or a flow as it comes into equilibrium with its surroundings. The surroundings, called the **dead state**, are usually taken as T0 = 298.15 K and 101.325 kPa [1, 2]. For a flowing stream the specific flow exergy is ψ = (h − h0) − T0(s − s0) + V²/2 + gz. Heat Q available at temperature T carries exergy Q(1 − T0/T). A megajoule of heat at 1,500 K is therefore worth 0.80 MJ of work, while a megajoule at 40 °C (313 K) is worth only 0.05 MJ. Electricity and shaft work are pure exergy. Unlike energy, exergy is not conserved. The **exergy destroyed** in any process equals T0·S_gen, a result known as the Gouy–Stodola theorem [1, 2].

The two accountings paint different pictures of the same plant. An energy balance on a coal-fired steam plant shows the largest outflow, more than half the fuel energy, leaving through the condenser into cooling water a few degrees above ambient. An exergy balance shows that this heat was worth little; at 40 °C its exergy is under 5 percent of its energy. The largest exergy destruction happens in the boiler, where combustion turns the fuel’s chemical exergy into hot gas, and that gas then gives up its heat across a gap of many hundreds of kelvin to steam [2]. Fuel itself counts as nearly pure exergy, since the chemical exergy of natural gas is close to its heating value [2]. This is why the history of power engineering is a history of raising steam temperatures and, as Section 2.4 shows, of sending high-temperature heat through a gas turbine before it ever reaches steam.

keyTerms.def: Energy is conserved; for a steady-flow device, heat in minus work out equals the change in enthalpy plus kinetic and potential energy of the flow.
A property, in J/K, defined by dS = δQ_rev/T, that measures how energy is dispersed and that can be created but never destroyed.
The entropy created inside a process by irreversibilities such as friction, mixing, combustion and heat transfer across a temperature difference; zero only for reversible processes.
The maximum useful work obtainable from a system or flow as it comes into equilibrium with a specified environment (the dead state).
Work potential lost in a real process, equal to the environment temperature T0 times the entropy generated.
The reference environment for exergy, usually 298.15 K and 101.325 kPa, at which a system can do no further work.

example.title: Worked example: the work potential lost when the boiler gas heats the steam
steps: Set up: 1,000 kJ of heat passes from combustion gas at 1,500 K to steam at 800 K. Take the environment as T0 = 298.15 K. Treat both as reservoirs at fixed temperature.
Entropy change of the gas: ΔS_gas = −Q/T = −1,000 kJ / 1,500 K = −0.667 kJ/K. Entropy change of the steam: ΔS_steam = +1,000 kJ / 800 K = +1.250 kJ/K.

Entropy generated: S_gen = 1.250 kJ/K − 0.667 kJ/K = 0.583 kJ/K. It is positive, as the second law requires; heat flowing the other way, from 800 K to 1,500 K, would give −0.583 kJ/K and is forbidden.
Exergy destroyed: X_dest = T0·S_gen = 298.15 K × 0.583 kJ/K = 174 kJ.
Check with the exergy of heat: at 1,500 K, 1,000 kJ × (1 − 298.15/1,500) = 801 kJ; at 800 K, 1,000 kJ × (1 − 298.15/800) = 627 kJ. The difference, 801 kJ − 627 kJ = 174 kJ, matches.
Interpret: all 1,000 kJ of energy arrived in the steam, but 174 kJ of the 801 kJ of work potential (22 percent) vanished in the transfer.
example.takeaway: Heat transfer across a large temperature gap conserves energy but destroys exergy, which is why boilers, not condensers, dominate a steam plant’s second-law losses.

misconception.myth: Energy is conserved, so a power plant that throws away more than half its fuel energy is just badly engineered; better design could turn nearly all of it into electricity.
misconception.fact: The first law allows that, but the second law does not. A cycle that takes in heat must reject enough heat to carry away the entropy that came in, Q_C ≥ Q_H·T_C/T_H. Good engineering reduces the extra entropy generated, but no design removes the rejection itself.

practice.q: A condenser receives 400 kg/s of wet steam at h = 2,300 kJ/kg and discharges saturated liquid at h = 190 kJ/kg. Neglecting kinetic and potential energy, how much heat goes to the cooling water?
choices: 844 MW
920 MW
76 MW
practice.explanation: Q = ṁ(h_in − h_out) = 400 kg/s × (2,300 − 190) kJ/kg = 844,000 kJ/s = 844 MW. 920 MW uses only the inlet enthalpy, 76 MW uses only the outlet enthalpy, and 2.11 MW forgets the mass flow and confuses kJ/kg with MW.

practice.q: A district heating network delivers 1 kWh of heat as water at 80 °C. With the environment at 25 °C, how much exergy does that heat carry, in kWh? What does your answer imply about heating buildings with electric resistance heaters?
practice.answer: Exergy = Q(1 − T0/T) = 3.6 MJ × (1 − 298.15 K/353.15 K) = 3.6 MJ × 0.156 = 0.56 MJ = 0.156 kWh. A resistance heater turns 1 kWh of electricity, which is pure exergy, into heat worth only about 0.16 kWh of work, destroying about 84 percent of the exergy. A device that used the electricity’s work potential to move heat, rather than to make it, could deliver far more heat per kWh; that device is the heat pump, which returns in Chapter 8.
practice.explanation: A good answer converts both temperatures to kelvin, gets about 0.16 kWh, and concludes that resistance heating is efficient by the first law (about 100 percent) but poor by the second law.

practice.q: An exergy analysis of a coal-fired steam plant finds the largest exergy destruction in which component?
choices: The condenser, because it rejects the most energy
The boiler, through combustion and heat transfer across a large temperature difference
The feedwater pump, because it handles the highest pressure
The generator, because it converts shaft work to electricity
practice.explanation: Combustion and the heat transfer from gas at roughly 1,500 K to steam at a few hundred kelvin generate most of the entropy. The condenser rejects the most energy, but that heat is near ambient temperature and carries little exergy. Pumps and generators lose only a few percent of their small or already-converted flows.

sections.title: The Carnot limit
reading: Sadi Carnot published *Réflexions sur la puissance motrice du feu* in Paris in 1824, at his own expense, in an edition of 600 copies [1, 2]. He reasoned with the caloric theory of his day, which treated heat as an indestructible fluid, and compared a heat engine with a waterwheel: work comes from caloric “falling” from a high temperature to a low one, as water falls from a high level to a low one. The caloric theory was wrong, but Carnot’s central conclusion survived its overthrow. The maximum work obtainable from heat depends only on the temperatures of the bodies between which it flows, not on the working substance [2]. Émile Clapeyron restated the argument in mathematical form in 1834, and in the early 1850s Clausius and William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, reconciled it with the conservation of energy [2].

The modern derivation takes three lines. An engine takes heat Q_H from a reservoir at T_H, does work W and rejects Q_C to a reservoir at T_C. The first law gives W = Q_H − Q_C. The entropy balance from Section 2.1 gives Q_C = T_C(Q_H/T_H + S_gen). Substituting, W = Q_H(1 − T_C/T_H) − T_C·S_gen [3]. The first term is the most work any engine could deliver; the second is the work lost to irreversibility, and it is never negative. Dividing by Q_H gives the **Carnot efficiency**, η_C = 1 − T_C/T_H, reached only by a fully reversible engine with S_gen = 0. Figure 2.1 shows the bookkeeping for steam at 823 K and a condenser at 319 K. The limit is 61 percent, and the ideal steam cycle analyzed in Section 2.3 reaches 41 percent.

Both temperatures must be **absolute temperatures**, in kelvin, because the derivation divides heat by temperature and entropy is measured from absolute zero. The Celsius error is large and common. For steam at 600 °C and a condenser at 33 °C, 1 − 33/600 gives an impossible 94.5 percent. The correct value is 1 − 306.15 K/873.15 K = 0.649, or 64.9 percent [3]. The formula also shows where effort pays. The derivative of η_C with respect to T_H is T_C/T_H², while with respect to T_C it is −1/T_H, so a kelvin removed from the cold side is worth more than a kelvin added to the hot side. In practice T_C is pinned near the temperature of the available cooling water or air, so designers push T_H upward until they reach the limits of steels and turbine alloys.

Real plants sit well below their Carnot limits. The U.S. Energy Information Administration publishes fleet-average **heat rates**, the fuel energy used per kilowatt-hour generated, on a higher-heating-value basis for fossil fuels (for nuclear plants, the reactor heat). In 2024 they were 10,777 Btu/kWh for coal plants, 10,443 Btu/kWh for nuclear plants and 7,754 Btu/kWh for natural gas plants [4]. Since 1 kWh = 3,412 Btu, the corresponding efficiencies are 3,412/10,777 = 31.7 percent for coal, 3,412/10,443 = 32.7 percent for nuclear and 3,412/7,754 = 44.0 percent for gas. Nuclear plants do only about as well as coal despite a completely different heat source, because light-water reactors raise steam at under 300 °C, which keeps T_H low. Gas leads because much of the gas fleet is combined-cycle, the subject of Section 2.4.

The gap between real and Carnot efficiency has identifiable causes. A Carnot engine takes in all its heat at T_H and rejects all of it at T_C, with no temperature difference between the working fluid and the reservoirs. A real engine takes in heat over a range of temperatures, needs finite temperature differences to move heat at a useful rate, and loses work to friction and pressure drops. Curzon and Ahlborn showed in 1975 that an engine whose only irreversibility is finite-rate heat transfer, operated for maximum power output, has efficiency 1 − √(T_C/T_H) [5]. For T_H = 873 K and T_C = 306 K that gives 40.8 percent, close to what good steam plants achieve. The Carnot formula is a ceiling, not a forecast. A better measure of engineering quality is the **second-law efficiency**, η/η_C.

keyTerms.def: A body large enough that it can supply or absorb heat without its temperature changing.
The maximum fraction of heat that any engine can convert to work between reservoirs at T_H and T_C, η_C = 1 − T_C/T_H with temperatures in kelvin.
Temperature measured from absolute zero, in kelvin (K = °C + 273.15); the only scale on which ratios of temperatures have physical meaning.
Fuel energy consumed per unit of electricity generated, for example Btu/kWh or kJ/kWh; its inverse, after unit conversion, is the efficiency.
Actual efficiency divided by the reversible (Carnot) efficiency for the same temperatures, a measure of how close a design comes to the physical limit.

example.title: Worked example: the Carnot ceiling for one kilowatt-hour from steam
steps: Convert to kelvin: steam at 600 °C gives T_H = 600 + 273.15 = 873.15 K; a condenser at 33 °C (the saturation temperature at 5 kPa) gives T_C = 33 + 273.15 = 306.15 K.
Minimum heat for 1 kWh of work: Q_H,min = 3.6 MJ / 0.649 = 5.54 MJ. Minimum heat rejected: 5.54 MJ − 3.60 MJ = 1.94 MJ.
Compare the 2024 U.S. coal fleet: 10,777 Btu/kWh × 1.055 kJ/Btu = 11,370 kJ/kWh = 11.37 MJ per kWh (HHV basis), so η = 3.6 MJ / 11.37 MJ = 0.317, and 11.37 − 3.60 = 7.77 MJ is rejected for every kWh.

Second-law efficiency: 0.317 / 0.649 = 0.49. The average coal plant burns 11.37 / 5.54 = 2.05 times the Carnot minimum heat. (Part of the gap comes from heating-value accounting and from fleet units with lower steam temperatures than 600 °C.)
example.takeaway: Even a perfect engine between 600 °C and 33 °C must reject 1.94 MJ for each kWh; real coal plants reject four times that, and most of the difference is irreversibility that engineering can attack.

misconception.myth: No machine can beat the Carnot efficiency, so wind turbines, solar cells and fuel cells must be Carnot-limited too.
misconception.fact: The Carnot limit applies to heat engines, devices that turn heat into work. A wind turbine extracts kinetic energy from moving air and is bounded by the Betz limit; a solar cell converts photons and is bounded by the Shockley–Queisser limit (both in Chapter 5). A fuel cell converts chemical energy directly and is bounded by the Gibbs free energy of its reaction, not by any temperature ratio.

practice.q: A geothermal binary plant receives heat from brine at 150 °C and rejects heat at 25 °C. What is its Carnot limit?
choices: 83.3 percent
29.5 percent
16.7 percent
54.0 percent
practice.explanation: η_C = 1 − 298.15 K / 423.15 K = 0.295. The value 83.3 percent comes from 1 − 25/150 in Celsius, and 16.7 percent is 25/150. Low-temperature resources have low ceilings, which is why geothermal plants convert only a modest fraction of their heat.

practice.q: Starting from T_H = 873.15 K and T_C = 306.15 K, which raises the Carnot efficiency more: raising T_H by 50 K, or lowering T_C by 50 K? Show both numbers, then explain why plant designers nevertheless concentrate on the hot side.
practice.answer: Baseline η_C = 1 − 306.15/873.15 = 0.649. Raising T_H to 923.15 K gives 1 − 306.15/923.15 = 0.668 (+1.9 points). Lowering T_C to 256.15 K gives 1 − 256.15/873.15 = 0.707 (+5.7 points). The cold side is more sensitive because ∂η/∂T_C = −1/T_H is larger in magnitude than ∂η/∂T_H = T_C/T_H². But T_C cannot fall below the temperature of the environment that absorbs the heat; a condenser at −17 °C would need refrigeration costing more work than it gained. T_H can be raised with better materials, so that is where effort goes.
practice.explanation: A strong answer computes both cases in kelvin, identifies the cold side as more sensitive, and explains that the environment fixes the practical floor for T_C.

practice.q: A vendor claims a new steam plant converts 70 percent of its heat to work, with steam at 560 °C and cooling at 30 °C. What should you conclude?
choices: The claim is plausible for an ultra-supercritical plant
The claim is plausible only with reheat
The claim is impossible, because the Carnot limit for these temperatures is about 64 percent
The claim cannot be checked without the steam pressure
practice.explanation: η_C = 1 − 303.15 K / 833.15 K = 0.636. No engine between these temperatures can exceed 63.6 percent, whatever its pressure, cycle or working fluid, so 70 percent violates the second law.

sections.title: Rankine and Brayton cycles
reading: Most of the world’s thermal electricity, from coal, nuclear, geothermal and solar-thermal plants, comes from the **Rankine cycle**. It is named for William John Macquorn Rankine, Regius Professor of Civil Engineering and Mechanics at Glasgow, whose 1859 *Manual of the Steam Engine and Other Prime Movers* set out the thermodynamics of steam power for engineers [1]. The ideal cycle has four processes, numbered as in Figure 2.2. From 1 to 2 a pump raises saturated liquid from condenser pressure to boiler pressure. From 2 to 3 the boiler heats, boils and superheats the water at constant pressure. From 3 to 4 the steam expands through a turbine, ideally at constant entropy. From 4 to 1 the condenser turns the wet exhaust back into liquid at constant pressure, rejecting heat to cooling water [2].

The Rankine cycle’s great advantage is the pump. Compressing a liquid takes very little work because its specific volume is tiny, and for an incompressible liquid w_p = v(P2 − P1). Water at 10 kPa has v = 0.00101 m³/kg, so raising it to 10 MPa takes 0.00101 m³/kg × 9,990 kPa = 10.1 kJ/kg, against about 1,360 kJ/kg delivered by the turbine. The **back work ratio**, pump or compressor work divided by turbine work, is under 1 percent [2]. Operating conditions have climbed steadily. Supercritical units run above water’s critical pressure of 22.06 MPa, where there is no boiling plateau at all, and many plants reheat the steam partway through the expansion [2]. Condensers commonly run at about 5 to 10 kPa, where water condenses at 33 to 46 °C, depending on the cooling water or air available.

Why does an ideal Rankine cycle with steam at 550 °C reach only about 41 percent, when the Carnot limit between 550 °C and 46 °C is 61 percent? The T-s diagram in Figure 2.2 shows the answer. Much of the heat enters while the water is warming as a liquid and while it boils at 311 °C, far below the superheat peak. Because q_in = ∫T ds along the constant-pressure heating line, the cycle performs exactly like a Carnot engine operating at the **mean temperature of heat addition**, T̄_H = q_in/(s3 − s2). In the worked example below T̄_H is only 540 K (267 °C), and the efficiency equals 1 − T_C/T̄_H [2]. Every classic improvement to steam plants, including higher boiler pressure, reheat, and regenerative feedwater heating with steam bled from the turbine, works by raising T̄_H or lowering T_C.

The gas turbine follows the **Brayton cycle**, named for the American engineer George Brayton, who built constant-pressure combustion engines in the 1870s. Air is compressed, fuel burns in it at nearly constant pressure, and the hot gas expands through a turbine and leaves as exhaust, so the real machine runs an open cycle. For an ideal cycle with air as a perfect gas, efficiency depends only on the **pressure ratio** r_p: η_B = 1 − r_p^(−(k−1)/k), where k = c_p/c_v ≈ 1.4 [2]. At r_p = 20 this gives 1 − 20^(−0.286) = 57.5 percent. The weak point is the compressor. Compressing a gas takes far more work than pumping a liquid, so even the ideal cycle at r_p = 20 between 288 K and 1,873 K spends 36 percent of the turbine’s work driving its own compressor, and component losses then cut deeply into the net output [2].

That is why gas-turbine progress is measured in firing temperature and component efficiency. Take r_p = 20, air entering at 288 K, a turbine inlet temperature of 1,873 K (1,600 °C), isentropic efficiencies of 0.88 for the compressor and 0.90 for the turbine, and c_p = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K). The compressor absorbs 445 kJ/kg, the turbine delivers 974 kJ/kg, and the net 529 kJ/kg divided by the 1,147 kJ/kg of heat added gives 46 percent, with a back work ratio of 0.46 and exhaust leaving at about 630 °C. Current heavy-duty H- and J-class machines fire at around 1,600 °C, hotter than their nickel-superalloy blades could survive uncooled, and they depend on internal air cooling and ceramic thermal barrier coatings [3]. Real machines also bleed cooling air and lose pressure in ducts, so their simple-cycle efficiencies are lower than this estimate; GE, for example, rates its 60 Hz 7HA.03 at 43.3 percent net (LHV).

keyTerms.def: A vapor power cycle of pumping, constant-pressure heating and boiling, expansion in a turbine, and constant-pressure condensation.
A gas power cycle of compression, constant-pressure heat addition, expansion in a turbine, and constant-pressure heat rejection (or, in practice, exhaust).
The fraction of turbine work consumed by the pump or compressor; under 1 percent in steam cycles and close to half in gas turbines.
The heat added divided by the entropy rise of the working fluid, T̄_H = q_in/Δs, which sets the efficiency of an ideal cycle as 1 − T_C/T̄_H.
Returning partly expanded steam to the boiler to raise its temperature again before further expansion, which raises efficiency and keeps turbine exhaust drier.
The ratio of compressor outlet pressure to inlet pressure in a gas turbine, which sets the ideal Brayton efficiency.

example.title: Worked example: an ideal Rankine cycle at 10 MPa and 550 °C
steps: State 1, saturated liquid at 10 kPa (45.81 °C), from steam tables: h1 = 191.81 kJ/kg, v1 = 0.001010 m³/kg, s1 = 0.6492 kJ/(kg·K).
Check with the mean temperature: T̄_H = 3,300.1 kJ/kg ÷ (6.7585 − 0.6492) kJ/(kg·K) = 540.2 K, and 1 − 318.96 K/540.2 K = 0.410. The Carnot limit between 823.15 K and 318.96 K is 0.613.
Per kilowatt-hour: 3,600 kJ ÷ 1,351.5 kJ/kg = 2.66 kg of steam must circulate for each kWh, and 2.66 kg × (2,140.4 − 191.8) kJ/kg = 5.19 MJ is rejected in the condenser.
example.takeaway: Even with no friction at all, a steam cycle reaches only two-thirds of its Carnot limit, because most of its heat enters at temperatures far below the peak.

misconception.myth: Our boiler makes steam at 550 °C, so the plant is a 550 °C heat engine and its efficiency should be close to the Carnot value for 550 °C.
misconception.fact: Only the last of the heat is added at 550 °C. In the ideal cycle at 10 MPa the mean temperature of heat addition is 267 °C, so even with no losses the efficiency is 41 percent, not 61 percent. Peak temperature tells you the ceiling; mean temperature tells you the performance.

practice.q: Why is the back work ratio of a Rankine cycle (under 1 percent) so much smaller than that of a gas turbine (close to half)?
choices: Steam turbines are more efficient than gas turbines
The Rankine cycle has a much lower pressure ratio
Water has a higher specific heat than air
The pump compresses a liquid, whose specific volume is roughly a thousand times smaller than a gas’s, and compression work is ∫v dP
practice.explanation: Compression work scales with specific volume. Liquid water at 0.001 m³/kg needs about 10 kJ/kg to reach 10 MPa, while air must be compressed as a gas. The Rankine pressure ratio is actually far larger (1,000 to 1 in the worked example), and turbine efficiency or specific heat do not explain the difference.

practice.q: An aeroderivative gas turbine has a pressure ratio of 15. Compute its ideal (cold-air-standard) Brayton efficiency with k = 1.4, and give two reasons the real machine will fall short of it.
practice.answer: η_B = 1 − 15^(−0.4/1.4) = 1 − 15^(−0.2857) = 1 − 0.461 = 0.539, or 53.9 percent. A real machine falls short because the compressor and turbine are not isentropic (an efficiency loss in the compressor raises its work, and in the turbine lowers its output, and the large back work ratio amplifies both); some compressed air bypasses combustion to cool the turbine blades; there are pressure drops in the combustor and ducts; and the gas properties (c_p and k) change with temperature and composition.
practice.explanation: A complete answer gets about 54 percent and names at least two real effects, ideally noting that a high back work ratio makes net output sensitive to component losses.

practice.q: The worked example ends with turbine exhaust that is 18.5 percent liquid (x4 = 0.815), wetter than turbine designers like. Which change makes the exhaust drier?
choices: Lowering the condenser pressure
Raising the boiler pressure at the same turbine inlet temperature
Reheating the steam partway through the expansion
Using a more efficient pump
practice.explanation: Reheating at 2 MPa back to 550 °C moves the expansion to higher entropy and raises the exit quality to about 0.92. Lowering condenser pressure and raising boiler pressure at fixed temperature both make the exhaust wetter. The pump does not affect turbine exit quality.

sections.title: Combined cycles and cogeneration
reading: Section 2.3 ended with a mismatch. The gas turbine takes in heat at a very high temperature but throws it away hot, at around 600 °C. The steam cycle rejects heat close to ambient but takes it in at a low mean temperature. A **combined cycle** stacks the two. The gas turbine is the **topping cycle**, and its exhaust flows through a **heat-recovery steam generator** (HRSG) that raises steam for a Rankine **bottoming cycle**, as in Figure 2.3 [1]. In large plants the HRSG produces steam at three pressure levels, with reheat, so that the water and steam temperatures follow the cooling exhaust closely and less exergy is destroyed in the heat transfer [1]. The plant as a whole then takes in heat at the gas turbine’s high temperatures, from compressor discharge up to the firing temperature, and rejects it near the condenser’s temperature, capturing the best end of each cycle.

The combined efficiency follows from a short energy balance. Let the fuel supply heat Q to the gas turbine, which delivers W_B = η_B·Q and rejects (1 − η_B)·Q in its exhaust. If all of that rejected heat reaches the steam cycle and the steam cycle converts a fraction η_R of it to work, then W_R = η_R(1 − η_B)·Q. Adding the outputs and dividing by Q gives η_cc = η_B + η_R(1 − η_B) [1, 2]. The relation rests on assumptions worth stating: all heat rejected by the gas turbine is offered to the steam cycle; the steam cycle receives no other heat, so there is no supplementary firing in the HRSG; both efficiencies refer to the same fuel heating value; and auxiliary loads are treated consistently. In practice some exhaust heat escapes through the stack, so η_R is best read as an effective efficiency from exhaust heat to steam-turbine work.

This relation explains how combined cycles moved past every other thermal plant. GE rates its 7HA.03 gas turbine at 43.3 percent in simple cycle and at more than 64 percent in combined cycle, both net on a lower-heating-value (LHV) basis. Solving for the bottoming cycle gives η_R = (0.64 − 0.433)/(1 − 0.433) = 0.365, so a steam cycle with an effective efficiency of only 36.5 percent adds 21 points. Measured records sit close to such ratings. In 2016 EDF’s Bouchain plant in France, built around a GE 9HA.01, was certified at 62.22 percent net, and in 2018 Chubu Electric’s Nishi-Nagoya Block 1 was recognized at 63.08 percent gross. Fleet averages are lower. U.S. gas combined-cycle units had average tested heat rates of about 7,600 Btu/kWh (HHV) from 2014 to 2021, about 45 percent on that basis (roughly 50 percent LHV); the gap from the ratings comes mainly from the many older, less efficient units in the fleet, with ambient conditions and wear adding to it [3].

Even a combined cycle rejects about a third of its fuel energy as low-temperature heat through its condenser and stack. **Cogeneration**, or combined heat and power (CHP), uses that heat for industrial process steam, district heating or hot water. The price is electrical output: to deliver useful heat at, say, 120 °C, a steam turbine must exhaust at a higher pressure and temperature than a condensing turbine, so each kilogram of steam does less work [2]. CHP performance is often summarized by the **utilization factor**, ε_u = (W_net + Q_useful)/Q_fuel. Actual cogeneration plants reach utilization factors as high as about 80 percent when there is a steady demand for the heat [2]. That number, however, adds electricity and heat as if a joule of each were equally valuable, which Section 2.1 showed they are not.

An exergy view puts CHP on a fair footing. Heat at 120 °C has an exergy factor of 1 − 298.15 K/393.15 K = 0.24. A CHP plant that turns 100 MJ of fuel into 30 MJ of electricity and 50 MJ of useful heat at 120 °C has a utilization factor of 80 percent but an exergy efficiency of about (30 + 50 × 0.24)/100 = 42 percent, taking the fuel’s exergy as roughly its heating value [2]. The practical test is the fuel saved compared with making the same products separately. With a 60 percent combined cycle and a 90 percent boiler, separate production takes 30/0.60 + 50/0.90 = 105.6 MJ, so CHP saves only 5 percent. Against a 35 percent coal plant the saving is 1 − 100/(85.7 + 55.6) = 29 percent. CHP pays most where the electricity it displaces is inefficient and the heat demand is steady.

sources.supports: Combined-cycle configuration, multi-pressure reheat heat-recovery steam generators, and the energy balance of topping and bottoming cycles.

sources.citation: Çengel, Y. A., Boles, M. A., & Kanoğlu, M. (2019). Thermodynamics: An engineering approach (9th ed.). McGraw-Hill Education.
sources.supports: Combined gas-vapor power cycles, cogeneration, the utilization factor and its typical values in real plants, and exergy of heat.

sources.supports: Table 8.2: average tested heat rates of U.S. natural gas combined-cycle units, about 7,600 Btu/kWh from 2014 to 2021.

keyTerms.def: A power plant in which a gas-turbine (Brayton) topping cycle’s exhaust heat drives a steam (Rankine) bottoming cycle.
The heat exchanger that raises steam from gas-turbine exhaust, usually at several pressure levels, in a combined-cycle plant.
In a stacked plant, the cycle that receives the high-temperature heat (topping) and the cycle that runs on the heat the first one rejects (bottoming).
Producing electricity and useful heat from one fuel input, so that heat an ordinary plant would reject serves a heating load.
Net electricity plus useful heat divided by fuel energy; a first-law measure for CHP plants that treats heat and work as equal.
Fuel energy with the water in the exhaust left as vapor (LHV) or condensed (HHV); for natural gas the HHV is about 11 percent higher than the LHV.

example.title: Worked example: a best-in-class H-class combined-cycle plant and one kilowatt-hour
steps: Data, net and LHV: gas turbine η_B = 0.433 (the 7HA.03 rating) and effective bottoming efficiency η_R = 0.365, which together match the plant rating of 0.64; these are new-plant, full-load ratings, whereas Chapter 1’s 500 MW reference plant uses a more conservative in-service 55 percent.
Per 100 MJ of fuel: the gas turbine makes 0.433 × 100 MJ = 43.3 MJ of work and sends (1 − 0.433) × 100 MJ = 56.7 MJ to the HRSG; the steam cycle turns 0.365 × 56.7 MJ = 20.7 MJ of that into work.
Combined efficiency: η_cc = 0.433 + 0.365 × (1 − 0.433) = 0.433 + 0.207 = 0.640. The steam turbine supplies 20.7/64.0 = 32 percent of the plant’s output.

Fuel per kilowatt-hour: 3,600 kJ / 0.640 = 5,625 kJ/kWh (LHV). Converting to the HHV basis used by EIA (natural gas HHV/LHV ≈ 1.11): 5,625 × 1.11 = 6,240 kJ/kWh, or 6,240 / 1.055 = 5,915 Btu/kWh, well below the U.S. combined-cycle fleet’s roughly 7,600 Btu/kWh.
Against simple cycle: the gas turbine alone needs 3,600 kJ / 0.433 = 8,314 kJ/kWh, so adding the bottoming cycle cuts fuel per kWh by 1 − 5,625/8,314 = 32 percent, with no extra fuel burned.
example.takeaway: A bottoming cycle that converts only about a third of the exhaust heat still raises plant efficiency from 43 to 64 percent, because that heat would otherwise be thrown away.

misconception.myth: Our CHP plant is 80 percent efficient, so it beats any combined-cycle plant at 60 percent.
misconception.fact: The 80 percent is a utilization factor that counts a joule of 120 °C heat as equal to a joule of electricity. On an exergy basis that CHP plant is about 42 percent efficient. The fair comparison is fuel use against producing the same electricity and heat separately; against a modern combined cycle and a good boiler, CHP often saves only a few percent.

practice.q: An older plant pairs a gas turbine of 38 percent efficiency with a bottoming steam cycle of 33 percent effective efficiency. What is the combined-cycle efficiency?
choices: 71.0 percent
58.5 percent
54.5 percent
12.5 percent
practice.explanation: η_cc = 0.38 + 0.33 × (1 − 0.38) = 0.38 + 0.205 = 0.585. Adding the two efficiencies (71 percent) counts the fuel heat twice, since the steam cycle sees only the 62 percent the gas turbine rejects; 12.5 percent is their product.

practice.q: A hospital installs a gas-engine CHP unit that converts fuel into 35 percent electricity and 45 percent useful heat as hot water at 90 °C. Compute its utilization factor and its approximate exergy efficiency (environment 25 °C, fuel exergy taken as its heating value). Which number should the hospital quote when comparing with buying grid electricity, and why?
practice.answer: Utilization factor = 0.35 + 0.45 = 0.80. Exergy factor of heat at 90 °C = 1 − 298.15/363.15 = 0.179, so exergy efficiency ≈ 0.35 + 0.45 × 0.179 = 0.43. Neither number alone settles the comparison; the hospital should compute the fuel saved against producing the same electricity and heat separately (grid electricity at its real efficiency plus a boiler), and it should prefer the exergy efficiency over the utilization factor when comparing with other ways of making work.
practice.explanation: A good answer gets 80 percent and about 43 percent, explains that low-temperature heat carries little exergy, and proposes a fuel-saved comparison against a stated alternative.

practice.q: The relation η_cc = η_B + η_R(1 − η_B) assumes which of the following?
choices: The steam cycle and the gas turbine have equal efficiencies
Both cycles operate between the same two temperatures
All heat rejected by the gas turbine is offered to the steam cycle, which receives no other heat
The HRSG burns extra fuel to raise steam temperature
practice.explanation: The derivation feeds the gas turbine’s rejected heat, (1 − η_B)Q, to the steam cycle and nothing else. The efficiencies can differ, the cycles span different temperatures, and supplementary firing would add heat the formula does not count.

interactives.title: Energy audit or exergy audit?
interactives.intro: A plant manager running a coal-fired steam unit with an efficiency of about 35 percent wants to cut fuel use and asks where the losses are. Think through each question before revealing the answer.

steps.q: An energy balance shows that about 55 percent of the fuel energy leaves through the condenser into cooling water at around 40 °C. Is the condenser the place to look for savings?
steps.a: Not primarily. Heat at 313 K with an environment at 298 K has an exergy factor of 1 − 298.15/313.15 = 0.048. So 55 percent of the fuel energy carries only about 0.55 × 0.048 = 2.6 percent of the fuel’s exergy. Most of that heat must be rejected anyway to carry the cycle’s entropy out.

steps.q: Then where is the work potential being lost?
steps.a: In the boiler. Combustion destroys a large share of the fuel’s chemical exergy, and heat transfer from gas near 1,500 K to steam whose mean temperature of heat addition is far lower (540 K in the ideal cycle of Section 2.3) destroys more. The worked example in Section 2.1 found 174 kJ destroyed per 1,000 kJ moved across just part of that gap.

steps.q: What design changes follow from the exergy audit?
steps.a: Narrow the temperature gap at the hot end: raise steam pressure and temperature (supercritical and ultra-supercritical units), add reheat, and use regenerative feedwater heating so the boiler adds heat at a higher mean temperature. Or put the high-temperature heat through a gas turbine first, which is the combined cycle of Section 2.4.

interactives.title: Carnot limit explorer
interactives.intro: Set the hot and cold temperatures in degrees Celsius; the formula converts them to kelvin. Compare the correct Carnot limit with the wrong answer you get by forgetting to convert, and watch how much heat a perfect engine must still reject per kilowatt-hour.

outputs.label: Minimum heat input per kWh of work
Minimum heat rejected per kWh of work

interactives.takeaway: Only absolute temperatures give the right limit. A steam plant at 600 °C cannot beat about 65 percent, a gas turbine firing at 1,600 °C with 15 °C air about 85 percent, and a 150 °C geothermal source about 30 percent.

interactives.title: Put the Rankine cycle in order
interactives.intro: Starting from saturated liquid leaving the condenser (state 1), arrange the four processes of the ideal Rankine cycle in the order the water experiences them.
steps: Pump (1 to 2): saturated liquid is compressed from about 10 kPa to boiler pressure, taking only about 10 kJ/kg of work.
Boiler (2 to 3): heat is added at constant pressure as the water warms, boils and is superheated.
Turbine (3 to 4): the steam expands at constant entropy to condenser pressure, producing most of the cycle’s work.
Condenser (4 to 1): the wet steam condenses at constant pressure and temperature, rejecting heat to cooling water or air.
interactives.explain: The cycle alternates two constant-pressure processes (boiler and condenser) with two constant-entropy ones (pump and turbine). Because the pump handles liquid, its work is about 1 percent of the turbine’s, which is the Rankine cycle’s main advantage over the Brayton cycle.

interactives.title: Combined-cycle efficiency explorer
interactives.intro: Set the gas turbine’s efficiency and the steam bottoming cycle’s effective efficiency. The model uses η_cc = η_B + η_R(1 − η_B), assuming all gas-turbine exhaust heat is offered to the steam cycle and there is no supplementary firing.

outputs.label: Fuel per kWh, gas turbine alone
Share of output from the steam turbine

interactives.takeaway: Each extra point of gas-turbine efficiency adds only about 0.6 points to the combined value, because a better topping cycle leaves less heat for the bottoming cycle; watch the steam turbine’s share of output fall as η_B rises.

slides.title: Chapter 2: Thermodynamics of Conversion
bullets: The first and second laws: energy, entropy, exergy
The Carnot limit, in kelvin
Rankine and Brayton cycles with real numbers
Combined cycles and cogeneration
slides.notes: Chapter 1 showed how much primary energy ends up as rejected heat. Today we find out why, and how much of that loss is physics and how much is engineering.

slides.title: The first law: energy balances
bullets: Closed system: ΔE = Q − W
Steady flow: q − w = Δh + ΔV²/2 + gΔz
Turbine work ≈ h_in − h_out
Example: 100 kg/s × 1,100 kJ/kg = 110 MW
slides.notes: Every Sankey diagram in Chapter 1 is a first-law diagram. Enthalpy is the bookkeeping variable for flowing fluids; kinetic and potential terms rarely matter in power plants.

slides.title: The second law and entropy
bullets: Heat does not flow by itself from cold to hot (Clausius)
No cycle turns all heat from one reservoir into work (Kelvin–Planck)
ΔS = ∫δQ/T + S_gen, with S_gen ≥ 0
Rejected heat is the only exit for entropy
slides.notes: Write the cycle entropy balance on the board: Q_C/T_C = Q_H/T_H + S_gen. Everything else in the chapter follows from it.

slides.title: Exergy: the work in the energy
bullets: Exergy of heat: Q(1 − T0/T)
1 MJ at 1,500 K is worth 0.80 MJ; at 40 °C, 0.05 MJ
Exergy destroyed = T0·S_gen
Boilers destroy the most; condensers reject the most
slides.notes: Energy and exergy audits rank losses differently. The boiler example, with 174 kJ destroyed per 1,000 kJ transferred, shows why steam temperatures keep rising.

slides.title: The Carnot limit
bullets: η_C = 1 − T_C/T_H, in kelvin
600 °C and 33 °C: 64.9 percent, not 94.5
W = Q_H(1 − T_C/T_H) − T_C·S_gen
Cold side is more sensitive, but fixed by the environment
slides.notes: Carnot reached this conclusion in 1824 while still believing in caloric. Use Figure 2.1 to walk through the bookkeeping per 100 MJ.

slides.title: Real plants against the limit
bullets: U.S. 2024 heat rates (HHV): coal 10,777, nuclear 10,443, gas 7,754 Btu/kWh
Efficiencies: 31.7, 32.7 and 44.0 percent
Coal fleet burns about twice the Carnot minimum heat
Curzon–Ahlborn: 1 − √(T_C/T_H) at maximum power
slides.notes: Divide 3,412 by the heat rate. Nuclear is low because light-water reactors make relatively cool steam; gas is high because of combined cycles.

slides.title: The Rankine cycle
bullets: Pump, boiler, turbine, condenser
Pump work about 10 kJ/kg; back work ratio under 1 percent
Ideal cycle at 10 MPa, 550 °C, 10 kPa: 41.0 percent
Mean heat-addition temperature only 267 °C
slides.notes: Use Figure 2.2. The gap from 61 to 41 percent is not friction; it is where on the T-s diagram the heat enters.

slides.title: The Brayton cycle
bullets: Ideal η_B = 1 − r_p^(−(k−1)/k): 57.5 percent at r_p = 20
Back work ratio near one half
Firing near 1,600 °C needs blade cooling and coatings
Exhaust leaves around 600 °C
slides.notes: With realistic component efficiencies our model gave 46 percent and exhaust at 630 °C. That hot exhaust is the opening for the combined cycle.

slides.title: Combined cycles
bullets: Gas-turbine topping, steam bottoming via an HRSG
η_cc = η_B + η_R(1 − η_B)
Assumes all exhaust heat offered to the steam cycle, no supplementary firing
slides.notes: State the assumptions every time you use the formula. Records: Bouchain 62.22 percent net (2016), Nishi-Nagoya 63.08 percent gross (2018).

slides.title: Cogeneration
bullets: Use rejected heat for process steam or district heating
Utilization factor around 80 percent in good plants
Exergy efficiency much lower: heat at 120 °C is worth 24 percent
Judge by fuel saved against separate production
slides.notes: Against a modern combined cycle and a good boiler, CHP saves a few percent; against old coal plants, nearly 30 percent. The answer depends on the alternative.

slides.title: Summary
bullets: Rejected heat carries entropy out; it cannot be designed away
Carnot sets the ceiling, mean temperatures set ideal performance
Combined cycles reach above 60 percent by stacking two cycles
Exergy, not energy, ranks losses and values heat
slides.notes: Before the quiz, rework the Rankine and combined-cycle examples with your own numbers using the explorers.

quiz.q: Water enters a boiler at h = 200 kJ/kg and leaves as steam at h = 3,500 kJ/kg, at a flow of 50 kg/s. What is the rate of heat input?
choices: 165 MW
175 MW
3.3 MW
quiz.explanation: Q = ṁΔh = 50 kg/s × (3,500 − 200) kJ/kg = 165,000 kJ/s = 165 MW. 175 MW uses only the outlet enthalpy; 16.5 MW and 3.3 MW are slips of units or mass flow.

quiz.q: The exergy destroyed in a process is equal to:
choices: The environment temperature times the entropy generated
The heat transferred divided by the temperature
The enthalpy change of the working fluid
The work output minus the heat input
quiz.explanation: X_dest = T0·S_gen (the Gouy–Stodola theorem). Q/T is an entropy transfer, not a destruction, and the other expressions are first-law quantities.

quiz.q: A gas turbine fires at 1,600 °C and takes in air at 15 °C. What is the Carnot limit for these two temperatures?
choices: 43 percent
62 percent
85 percent
99 percent
quiz.explanation: η_C = 1 − 288.15 K / 1,873.15 K = 0.846. Using Celsius directly gives 99 percent. The real machine’s simple-cycle efficiency is around 43 percent, far below the limit, largely because its heat rejection happens at high exhaust temperatures.

quiz.q: Why must temperatures in the Carnot formula be in kelvin?
choices: Because SI rules require kelvin in all equations
Because Celsius temperatures can be negative
Because kelvin values are larger and give more accurate results
Because the formula comes from ratios of heat to temperature, which only make physical sense on a scale that starts at absolute zero
quiz.explanation: The derivation uses Q/T terms from the entropy balance. A ratio of temperatures only has meaning on an absolute scale; Celsius has an arbitrary zero, so ratios of Celsius values are meaningless.

quiz.q: Why does the Rankine cycle need so little pump work compared with the work a gas-turbine compressor needs?
choices: The pump runs at a lower pressure ratio
The pump compresses liquid water, whose specific volume is very small
The pump is driven by a separate motor
Water is incompressible, so compressing it needs no work at all
quiz.explanation: Pump work is v·ΔP, and liquid water has v ≈ 0.001 m³/kg, so about 10 kJ/kg suffices to reach 10 MPa. The pump work is small but not zero, and the Rankine pressure ratio is actually much higher than a gas turbine’s.

quiz.q: What is the ideal cold-air-standard efficiency of a Brayton cycle with a pressure ratio of 20 and k = 1.4?
choices: 75.0 percent
95.0 percent
42.5 percent
57.5 percent
quiz.explanation: η_B = 1 − 20^(−0.4/1.4) = 1 − 1/2.354 = 0.575. 42.5 percent is 1/2.354, the temperature ratio’s inverse, and 95 percent is 1 − 1/20, which ignores the exponent.

quiz.q: A gas turbine with 40 percent efficiency feeds an HRSG that recovers 90 percent of its exhaust heat for a steam cycle that converts 38 percent of the heat it receives. What is the combined efficiency?
choices: 60.5 percent
62.8 percent
78.0 percent
55.2 percent
quiz.explanation: Effective η_R = 0.90 × 0.38 = 0.342, so η_cc = 0.40 + 0.342 × 0.60 = 0.605. 62.8 percent ignores the stack loss, and 78 percent simply adds the two efficiencies.

quiz.q: Which statement about a CHP plant with a utilization factor of 80 percent is correct?
choices: It must use less fuel than any combination of separate plants
Its exergy efficiency is also 80 percent
Its exergy efficiency is lower, because useful low-temperature heat carries much less work potential than electricity
It violates the Carnot limit
quiz.explanation: The utilization factor counts heat and electricity equally. Heat at 120 °C, for example, has an exergy factor of about 0.24, so the exergy efficiency is far below 80 percent. Whether it saves fuel depends on the separate plants it is compared with, and it does not violate Carnot because most of its output is heat, not work.

challenge.title: Rankine cycle with and without reheat
challenge.prompt: An ideal steam cycle has turbine inlet conditions of 10 MPa and 550 °C and a condenser at 10 kPa. Using steam tables (for example, the tables in Çengel, Boles and Kanoğlu), compute the net work, heat input, thermal efficiency and turbine exit quality. Then modify the cycle so the steam expands to 2 MPa, is reheated to 550 °C, and expands again to 10 kPa, and compute the same four quantities. Explain the changes using the mean temperature of heat addition and say why designers adopt reheat even when the efficiency gain is modest.
challenge.deliverable: A table of state points (P, T, h, s, quality) for both cycles, the four results for each, and a paragraph of 150 to 250 words interpreting them.
rubric: Correct state data and pump work (about 10.1 kJ/kg) with units at every step
Without reheat: net work about 1,352 kJ/kg, efficiency about 41.0 percent, exit quality about 0.815
With reheat: net work about 1,652 kJ/kg, efficiency about 42.8 percent, exit quality about 0.923
Explains the gain through a higher mean temperature of heat addition and the drier turbine exhaust
Compares the results with the Carnot limit for 550 °C and 45.8 °C (about 61 percent)

challenge.title: Should the campus build a CHP plant?
challenge.prompt: A university campus needs 14 MW of electricity and 18 MW of heat as hot water at 120 °C, around the clock. Option A buys grid electricity and burns gas in a boiler of 90 percent efficiency. Option B installs a gas-turbine CHP unit that converts fuel into 35 percent electricity and 45 percent useful heat. Compute the fuel each option uses if the grid electricity comes from a 60 percent combined-cycle plant, and again if it comes from a 40 percent plant. For Option B, also compute the utilization factor and exergy efficiency (environment 25 °C). Recommend an option, and say what changes if most grid electricity comes from wind farms.
challenge.deliverable: A short calculation table for both grid cases, followed by a recommendation of 150 to 250 words.
rubric: Option B fuel: 40 MW; Option A fuel: 43.3 MW (60 percent grid) or 55.0 MW (40 percent grid), so savings of about 8 or 27 percent
Utilization factor 80 percent and exergy efficiency about 46 percent (0.35 + 0.45 × 0.24), with temperatures in kelvin
Explains that the value of CHP depends on the efficiency of the electricity it displaces
Recognizes that low-carbon grid electricity (for example from wind) weakens the case for gas CHP, and mentions alternatives such as heat pumps

review.by: Researched and written with web-search verification; then fact-checked independently by a second agent. Web search confirmed the EIA 2024 Table 8.1 heat rates, the EIA Table 8.2 combined-cycle tested heat rates, the GE 7HA.03 ratings (43.3 percent simple cycle, more than 64 percent combined), the Bouchain (62.22 percent net, 2016) and Nishi-Nagoya (63.08 percent gross, March 2018) records, and Carnot's 1824 edition (Bachelier, 118 pages, 600 copies, at his own expense). Bibliographic details for Clausius 1865, Curzon and Ahlborn 1975, Fox 1986, Mendoza 1960, Rankine 1859, and the Çengel, Moran and Gülen texts were checked by expert review. Every thermodynamic number was recomputed: steam states with CoolProp 8.0 (h3 3,502.0 kJ/kg, s3 6.7585, x4 0.8146, h4 2,140.4, η 0.4095, mean heat-addition temperature 540.2 K = 267 °C, reheat case η 0.428 and x 0.923), and the Brayton, Carnot, Curzon-Ahlborn, exergy, combined-cycle and CHP arithmetic by script. The SVG coordinates were checked against the stated data. Every answer key was re-solved blind.

corrections.before: U.S. gas combined-cycle units had average tested heat rates of about 7,600 Btu/kWh (HHV) from 2014 to 2021, about 45 percent, because real units run at part load, in hot weather and with aging parts [3].
corrections.after: U.S. gas combined-cycle units had average tested heat rates of about 7,600 Btu/kWh (HHV) from 2014 to 2021, about 45 percent on that basis (roughly 50 percent LHV); the gap from the ratings comes mainly from the many older, less efficient units in the fleet, with ambient conditions and wear adding to it [3].
corrections.why: The explanation leaves out the two largest causes. The fleet figure is HHV while the 64 percent rating is LHV: dividing by about 1.11 alone takes 64 percent down to about 58 percent. Most of the fleet is also F-class or older and was built long before the 7HA.03. Part load is a poor explanation for a tested heat rate. The EIA Table 8.2 values found by search (7,658, 7,655 and 7,652 Btu/kWh for 2014 to 2016) confirm the 'about 7,600' figure itself.

corrections.before: The U.S. Energy Information Administration publishes fleet-average **heat rates**, the fuel energy used per kilowatt-hour generated, on a higher-heating-value basis.
corrections.after: The U.S. Energy Information Administration publishes fleet-average **heat rates**, the fuel energy used per kilowatt-hour generated, on a higher-heating-value basis for fossil fuels (for nuclear plants, the reactor heat).
corrections.why: Nuclear fuel has no heating value. EIA's nuclear figure in Table 8.1 is a weighted average of tested heat rates for reactor thermal output, so 'higher-heating-value basis' applies only to the fossil rows. The 2024 values themselves (10,777, 10,443 and 7,754 Btu/kWh) were confirmed against EIA Table 8.1 by web search.

corrections.before: Nuclear plants do no better than coal despite a completely different heat source, because light-water reactors raise steam at under 300 °C, which keeps T_H low.
corrections.after: Nuclear plants do only about as well as coal despite a completely different heat source, because light-water reactors raise steam at under 300 °C, which keeps T_H low.
corrections.why: On the chapter's own numbers nuclear (32.7 percent) is one point better than coal (31.7 percent), so 'no better' is not literally true.

corrections.before: GE rates its 7HA.03 gas turbine at 43.3 percent in simple cycle and above 64 percent in a combined cycle with one gas and one steam turbine, both net on a lower-heating-value (LHV) basis.
corrections.after: GE rates its 7HA.03 gas turbine at 43.3 percent in simple cycle and at more than 64 percent in combined cycle, both net on a lower-heating-value (LHV) basis.
corrections.why: Search confirmed 43.3 percent net LHV simple cycle and GE's 'more than 64 percent' net combined-cycle claim. It did not tie that claim to the 1x1 configuration: launch reports gave 63.9 percent net, and the 1x1 and 2x1 ratings were quoted separately (640 MW and 1,282 MW). Removing the configuration detail keeps the sentence safe.

corrections.before: Worked example: our reference combined-cycle plant and one kilowatt-hour
corrections.after: Worked example: a best-in-class H-class combined-cycle plant and one kilowatt-hour
corrections.why: Chapter 1 defines 'a 500 MW combined-cycle gas plant, one of this book’s two reference plants' at 55 percent efficiency and says Chapter 2 explains how two cycles reach that figure. Calling a 64 percent 7HA.03 plant 'our reference combined-cycle plant' contradicts that, and nothing in Chapter 2 reconciles the two.

corrections.before: Data, net and LHV: gas turbine η_B = 0.433 (the 7HA.03 rating) and effective bottoming efficiency η_R = 0.365, which together match the plant rating of 0.64.
corrections.after: Data, net and LHV: gas turbine η_B = 0.433 (the 7HA.03 rating) and effective bottoming efficiency η_R = 0.365, which together match the plant rating of 0.64; these are new-plant, full-load ratings, whereas Chapter 1’s 500 MW reference plant uses a more conservative in-service 55 percent.
corrections.why: This states the difference from Chapter 1's 55 percent assumption explicitly, so learners do not read the two as conflicting values for the same plant.

corrections.before: The plant as a whole then takes in heat at the gas turbine’s firing temperature and rejects it at the condenser’s temperature, capturing the best end of each cycle.
corrections.after: The plant as a whole then takes in heat at the gas turbine’s high temperatures, from compressor discharge up to the firing temperature, and rejects it near the condenser’s temperature, capturing the best end of each cycle.
corrections.why: In a Brayton cycle heat is added from compressor-discharge temperature (about 730 K in the chapter's own example) up to the firing temperature, not at the firing temperature. Section 2.3 builds the whole lesson on the mean temperature of heat addition, so this shortcut undercuts it.

corrections.before: Utilization factor up to about 80 percent
corrections.after: Utilization factor around 80 percent in good plants
corrections.why: Çengel (the cited source) says actual cogeneration plants reach utilization factors 'as high as 80 percent' and that some recent plants go higher. Modern gas-engine and gas-turbine CHP often quotes 85 to 90 percent (LHV), so 'up to' wrongly implies a ceiling.

corrections.before: Combustion destroys a large share of the fuel’s chemical exergy, and heat transfer from gas near 1,500 K to steam whose mean temperature is only about 540 K destroys more.
corrections.after: Combustion destroys a large share of the fuel’s chemical exergy, and heat transfer from gas near 1,500 K to steam whose mean temperature of heat addition is far lower (540 K in the ideal cycle of Section 2.3) destroys more.
corrections.why: 540 K is the mean heat-addition temperature of the ideal 10 MPa non-reheat, non-regenerative cycle. A 35 percent coal unit with reheat and feedwater heating has a higher mean temperature, so the figure should be credited to the example rather than to this plant.

corrections.before: Heat at 120 °C has an exergy factor of about 0.24, so the exergy efficiency is far below 80 percent.
corrections.after: Heat at 120 °C, for example, has an exergy factor of about 0.24, so the exergy efficiency is far below 80 percent.
corrections.why: The question gives no heat temperature, so the explanation should present 120 °C as an example, not as part of the data.

review.summary: The chapter is highly accurate. Every recomputed number checks out: the Rankine state points and 41.0 percent efficiency, the 267 °C mean temperature, the Brayton model, the Carnot and Curzon-Ahlborn values, the combined-cycle and CHP arithmetic, the explorer formulas, and the T-s and Sankey proportions in the figures. All 16 keys are correct and all 15 sources are real and support their claims, so the corrections are mostly imprecisions, chiefly the explanation of the fleet heat-rate gap and the HHV/nuclear wording. It contradicts Chapter 1: Chapter 1's 500 MW reference combined-cycle plant runs at 55 percent, while Chapter 2's example calls a 64 percent 7HA.03 plant 'our reference combined-cycle plant' and never reconciles the two; the corrections retitle that example and add a sentence explaining the difference.
